name: Spanish Essentials
author: Recurse
subject: languages
description: Greetings, pronunciation, ser vs estar, articles, present-tense and stem-changing verbs, gustar, numbers and time.

lesson.intro: Spanish is the native language of nearly 500 million people and official in 20 countries. Here is the core of a first conversation: greeting people, saying who you are and how you feel, naming things, and the most common present-tense verbs.
objectives: Greet people and introduce yourself, choosing between tú and usted
Pronounce Spanish words from their spelling and place the stress
Choose between ser and estar, and make articles and adjectives agree
Conjugate regular, irregular and stem-changing verbs, and use gustar
Use numbers, the time, days and question words in a conversation

sections.title: Greetings and introductions
sections.key: Greet by the time of day, and use usted with strangers, older people and formal settings, keeping tú for friends, family and children.
sections.body:
Spanish greetings change with the time of day:

[[visual]]

Spanish has two ways to say "you". Use **tú** with friends, family, children and people your age in casual settings. Use **usted** with strangers, older people and in formal situations. Usted takes the same verb form as él (he) and ella (she):

[[visual 2]]

Written questions and exclamations open with an upside-down mark: ¿Cómo estás? ¡Hola!

[[visual 3]]

[[visual 4]]

visual.title: Greetings
rows: After dark; also to say goodbye

visual.title: Meeting someone
visual.caption: Hi! What's your name? / My name is Lucía. And you? / My name is Tom. Nice to meet you. / Likewise. How are you? / Fine, thanks.

sections.tip: Me llamo literally means "I call myself". Soy Lucía (I am Lucía) works too.
sections.pitfall: Using tú with someone you should address as usted. With a stranger or an older person, start with usted; they will tell you if tú is fine.

check.question: It is 4 p.m. and you walk into a shop. Which greeting fits best?
check.explanation: Buenas tardes covers the afternoon until dark. Buenos días is for the morning, and buenas días is wrong because día is masculine.

sections.title: Pronunciation, stress and accents
sections.key: Spanish spelling is regular: five pure vowels, a silent h, and stress that follows two rules, with a written accent marking every exception.
sections.body:
Spanish spelling is far more regular than English: learn a handful of rules and you can pronounce almost any word you read.

The five **vowels** are short and pure and never change: a as in father, e as in bet, i as in machine, o as in note (without the glide), u as in rule. So mesa is MEH-sah, never MEE-sa.

[[visual]]

**Stress** follows two rules, and a **written accent** marks every exception:

[[visual 2]]

Accents also tell apart words that are otherwise spelled the same: sí (yes) and si (if), tú (you) and tu (your), él (he) and el (the).

visual.title: Consonants to watch
rows: j, and g before e or i
g before a, o or u
s in Latin America; th as in thin in most of Spain
c before a, o or u
y as in yes in most regions; closer to sh in Argentina and Uruguay
España, mañana; año (year) is not ano
One quick tap, like the tt in American butter
rr, or r at the start

items.title: Ends in a vowel, n or s

sections.pitfall: Pronouncing the h or using English vowel sounds. Hola is OH-lah, and each vowel keeps its one pure sound in every word.

check.question: Which of these words is stressed on its last syllable?
check.explanation: Ciudad ends in d, a consonant other than n or s, so the stress falls on the last syllable: ciu-DAD. Casa ends in a vowel, and hablan and zapatos end in n and s, so all three stress the second-to-last syllable.

sections.title: Ser and estar: two verbs for "to be"
sections.key: Ser says what something is (identity, origin, job, traits, time); estar says where it is and how it is right now.
sections.body:
Spanish has two verbs that mean "to be", and they are not interchangeable.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Some adjectives change meaning with the verb: Juan **es** aburrido means Juan is boring (a trait), while Juan **está** aburrido means Juan is bored (right now).

items.title: Ser
points: Origin, with de: Es de Chile.
Profession, with no article: Mi padre es profesor.
Time: Son las tres. (It is three o'clock.)

items.title: Estar
items.sub: where it is and how it is now

sections.tip: The location of an event is an exception: La fiesta es en mi casa (the party is at my house) uses ser.
sections.pitfall: Choosing estar for anything that feels temporary. Time and event locations use ser (son las tres; la fiesta es en mi casa), while location uses estar even when permanent (Madrid está en España).

check.question: Which verb completes the sentence? Las llaves ___ en la mesa. (The keys are on the table.)
check.explanation: This is location, so it takes estar, and las llaves is plural, so the form is están. Son is the tempting choice, but ser does not describe where things are.

sections.title: Articles, gender and plurals
sections.key: Every noun is masculine or feminine, and its articles and adjectives match it in gender and number: las casas rojas.
sections.body:
Every Spanish noun is **masculine** or **feminine**, and the words around it must match.

[[visual]]

Nouns ending in -o are usually masculine and nouns ending in -a usually feminine, but common exceptions exist: el día (day), el mapa (map), el problema (problem), la mano (hand). Learn every noun with its article.

[[visual 2]]

Adjectives usually come after the noun and **agree** with it in gender and number: el libro rojo, la casa roja, los libros rojos, las casas rojas. Adjectives ending in -e or a consonant change only for number: un chico inteligente, una chica inteligente.

A group that mixes masculine and feminine uses the masculine plural, so los niños can mean boys, or boys and girls together.
sections.pitfall: Guessing a noun's gender from its meaning or ending alone. Learn every noun with its article: el problema and la mano both break the -o and -a pattern.

check.question: What is the plural of la ciudad (the city)?
check.explanation: Ciudad ends in a consonant, so it adds -es, and the feminine article la becomes las: las ciudades.

sections.title: Present tense: regular verbs, tener, ir, hacer
sections.key: Regular verbs drop -ar, -er or -ir and add a person ending, so the pronoun is usually dropped; tener, ir and hacer are irregular and must be memorized.
sections.body:
The dictionary form of a verb, the **infinitive**, ends in -ar, -er or -ir. To conjugate a regular verb, drop that ending and add the ending for the person:

[[visual]]

The ending already shows who is acting, so the subject pronoun is usually left out: Hablo español means I speak Spanish.

Three very common verbs are irregular:

[[visual 2]]

- **Tener** gives your age: Tengo veinte años (I am twenty; literally I have twenty years).
- **Ir a + infinitive** is the near future: Voy a comer (I am going to eat).
- **Hacer** gives the weather: Hace frío (it is cold), hace calor (it is hot). A person who feels cold says Tengo frío.

visual.caption: -er and -ir verbs share their endings except for nosotros and vosotros.

visual.title: Three irregular verbs
rows: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen
voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van
hago, haces, hace, hacemos, hacéis, hacen
visual.caption: Forms in order: yo, tú, él, nosotros, vosotros, ellos.

sections.tip: Vosotros (you all, informal) is used only in Spain. In Latin America, ustedes is used for every group.
sections.pitfall: Keeping the subject pronoun in every sentence. Yo hablo is correct but sounds emphatic; Hablo is normal, because the ending already says who.

check.question: Which form completes the sentence? Ellos ___ pan todos los días. (comer, to eat)
check.explanation: For -er verbs the ellos ending is -en, so comer becomes comen. Coman is the mistake of using the -an ending that belongs to -ar verbs.

sections.title: Stem-changing verbs and gustar
sections.key: Stem-changing verbs change a stressed stem vowel in every form except nosotros and vosotros, and gustar agrees with the thing liked: me gustan los perros.
sections.body:
Ask a Spanish speaker what they want and you hear quiero, not quero. Many common verbs take the regular endings but change a stem vowel whenever it is stressed:

[[visual]]

The change skips nosotros and vosotros, where the stress falls on the ending: teachers call it the **boot pattern**. Querer and poder take an infinitive: Quiero aprender español. ¿Puedes ayudarme?

**Gustar** works backward compared with "to like": me gusta el café means "coffee is pleasing to me". The thing liked is the subject, and a pronoun (me, te, le, nos, os, les) shows the person, so the verb agrees with the thing:

[[visual 2]]

Keep the article: me gusta el café, not me gusta café. **Encantar** (to love something) works the same way: Me encanta la playa.

visual.title: Stem-changing verbs
rows: quiero, quieres, quiere, queremos, queréis, quieren
pensar (to think), empezar (to begin), preferir (to prefer)
puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, podéis, pueden
dormir (to sleep), volver (to return), costar (to cost): ¿Cuánto cuesta?
juego, juegas, juega, jugamos, jugáis, juegan
pido, pides, pide, pedimos, pedís, piden
visual.caption: Forms in order: yo, tú, él, nosotros, vosotros, ellos.

visual.title: Gustar agrees with the thing liked
rows: A Ana le gustan las películas.
le: to her; a Ana says who

sections.pitfall: Saying yo gusto el café. Gustar agrees with the thing liked, and the person goes in the pronoun: me gusta el café, me gustan los libros.

check.question: Complete the sentence: Me ___ las manzanas. (I like apples.)
check.explanation: The subject is las manzanas, which is plural, so the verb is gustan. Gusta would fit a single thing (me gusta la manzana), and gusto would mean "I please", making the speaker the subject.

sections.title: Numbers, time and question words
sections.key: Numbers 16 to 29 are single words and later ones join with y; question words carry accents, and the time uses ser: es la una, son las tres.
sections.body:
Numbers 0 to 15 have their own names, 16 to 29 are written as one word, and from 31 the tens and units join with **y**:

[[visual]]

Question words carry a written accent:

[[visual 2]]

Telling the time uses ser: ¿Qué hora es? One o'clock is singular, **es la una**; every other hour is plural, **son las dos**. Add minutes with y and subtract them with menos: son las tres y media (3:30), son las cinco y cuarto (5:15), son las ocho menos diez (7:50).

[[visual 3]]

Days are masculine and lowercase, and the week starts on Monday. El lunes means on Monday; los lunes means on Mondays, every week.

visual.title: Counting to 100
rows: cero, uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco
treinta, cuarenta, cincuenta, sesenta, setenta, ochenta, noventa
treinta y uno, cuarenta y cinco

visual.title: Question words
rows: The answer porque (because) is one word, no accent
¿Cuántos años tienes? Tengo treinta y dos.

sections.tip: Uno becomes un before a masculine noun: un libro, veintiún años.
sections.pitfall: Forgetting the accent on question words. ¿Dónde? asks where, while donde without the accent links two parts of a statement; and porque (because) is not ¿por qué? (why).

check.question: Which question word asks "when?"
check.explanation: ¿Cuándo? means when. It is easy to confuse with ¿Cuánto? (how much), which differs by one letter.

keyTerms.definition: The two words for "you": tú is informal (friends, family, children); usted is formal (strangers, elders, work) and takes the él/ella verb form.
"To be" for what something is: identity, origin, profession, lasting traits and time (soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son).
"To be" for where something is and how it is right now: location, feelings, conditions (estoy, estás, está, estamos, estáis, están).
Every noun is masculine or feminine, and its articles and adjectives must match: el libro, la mesa.
Articles and adjectives change to match the noun in gender and number: las casas rojas.
The dictionary form of a verb, ending in -ar, -er or -ir: hablar, comer, vivir.
The everyday way to talk about the near future: Voy a comer (I am going to eat).
The mark on a vowel (á, é, í, ó, ú) that shows stress breaking the normal rules, or tells apart words such as sí (yes) and si (if).
A verb whose stem vowel changes when stressed (e → ie, o → ue, e → i) in every present form except nosotros and vosotros: quiero, puedo, pido.
"To be pleasing": the thing liked is the subject, so the verb agrees with it: me gusta el libro, me gustan los libros.

summary: Greet by time of day; usted for strangers, tú for friends.
Five pure vowels, a silent h, and an accent wherever stress breaks the rules.
Ser says what something is; estar says where it is and how it is now.
Articles and adjectives match the noun: las casas rojas.
Drop -ar, -er, -ir and add endings; stem-changers skip nosotros and vosotros.
Gustar agrees with the thing liked; the time uses ser: es la una, son las tres.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain when to use ser and when to use estar to a friend starting Spanish, with one example sentence for each.

questions.question: Translate into Spanish: Good morning.
questions.explanation: Buenos días is the standard morning greeting, used until around lunchtime. Día is masculine, so it is buenos, not buenas. Buen día is also common in parts of Latin America.

questions.question: Translate into Spanish, speaking to a friend: How are you?
questions.explanation: ¿Cómo estás? uses the tú form of estar, which suits a friend. With a stranger you would say ¿Cómo está usted? ¿Qué tal? is a casual alternative.

questions.question: How do you politely ask a stranger's name in Spanish?
questions.answer: ¿Cómo se llama usted? Usted is the formal "you" for strangers and older people; with a friend, ask ¿Cómo te llamas?
questions.explanation: Both questions use llamarse (to be called): the formal one uses se with the usted form, the informal one uses te with the tú form. Answer with Me llamo ... (My name is ...).

questions.question: Choose the right verb: Mi hermana ___ médica. (My sister is a doctor.)
questions.explanation: Professions use ser because they say what someone is, and es is the form for ella. Está would describe where she is or how she feels, not her job.

questions.question: Choose the right verb: Madrid ___ en España.
questions.explanation: Location uses estar, and Madrid takes the third-person singular form está. Es is the common mistake: ser says what something is, not where it is.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'Juan es aburrido' and 'Juan está aburrido'?
choices: They mean the same; está is just more formal
Es aburrido means he is bored now; está aburrido means he is boring
Es aburrido means he is boring; está aburrido means he is bored now
Está aburrido is wrong; aburrido only works with ser
questions.explanation: Ser gives a lasting trait (he is a boring person) and estar gives a current state (he is bored at the moment). Swapping the two meanings is the usual mix-up: estar is for how someone is right now.

questions.question: Translate into Spanish: I am from Mexico.
questions.explanation: Origin uses ser + de: soy de México. The pronoun yo is optional because soy already means "I am". Estoy de México is wrong because estar is not used for origin.

questions.question: Which phrase correctly says 'the red houses'?
questions.explanation: Casa is feminine, so the plural article is las and the adjective takes the feminine plural ending -as. Las casas rojos is the common slip: the adjective must match the noun too, not only the article.

questions.question: Which of these nouns takes el, even though it ends in -a?
questions.explanation: Día is masculine: el día, buenos días. Mesa, casa and semana follow the usual pattern and are feminine (la mesa, la casa, la semana). El mapa and el problema are other masculine nouns ending in -a.

questions.question: Make 'el lápiz' (the pencil) plural.
questions.explanation: A final -z changes to -c before -es is added, and el becomes los: los lápices. Lápizes is a common spelling mistake.

questions.question: Conjugate hablar (to speak) for yo.
questions.explanation: Drop -ar to get the stem habl- and add the yo ending -o: hablo. Hablas is the tú form and habla is the form for él or ella.

questions.question: Complete with escribir (to write): Tú ___ una carta.
questions.explanation: Escribir is a regular -ir verb, and the tú ending for -er and -ir verbs is -es: escribes. Escribís is the vosotros form, escribe is for él or ella, and escribas wrongly uses the -as ending of -ar verbs.

questions.question: Translate into Spanish: I am twenty years old.
questions.explanation: Spanish states age with tener: literally "I have twenty years". Soy veinte años is a common mistake copied from English. Write años with ñ if you can, since anos is a different word.

questions.question: Translate into Spanish: I am going to eat.
questions.explanation: Ir a + infinitive expresses the near future: voy (I go) + a + comer. Only ir is conjugated; voy a como is wrong because the second verb stays in the infinitive.

questions.question: How do you say 'It is cold' about the weather in Spanish?
questions.answer: Hace frío. Weather uses hacer (literally "it makes cold"). For a person who feels cold, use tener: Tengo frío.
questions.explanation: Spanish describes weather with hace: hace frío, hace calor, hace sol. Está frío describes a thing, such as cold coffee (el café está frío), not the weather.

questions.question: Write the number 23 in Spanish words.
questions.explanation: Numbers from 21 to 29 are single words: veinti- plus the unit, so veintiuno, veintidós, veintitrés. From 31 on, the tens and units are joined with y (treinta y tres).

questions.question: Translate the question word into Spanish: where?
questions.explanation: ¿Dónde? asks about place, as in ¿Dónde vives? (Where do you live?). Question words carry a written accent; donde without one is used in statements, as in la casa donde vivo.

questions.question: How do you ask 'How much does it cost?' in Spanish?
questions.answer: ¿Cuánto cuesta? For more than one item, ask ¿Cuánto cuestan?
questions.explanation: Cuánto means how much, and cuesta is the él/ella form of costar (to cost). It is one of the most useful phrases for shopping and travel.

questions.question: Match each Spanish expression to its meaning.
questions.explanation: These courtesy words come up in every conversation. De nada literally means "of nothing", and hasta luego is used even when you may not see the person again soon.

questions.question: Match each day of the week to its English name.
questions.explanation: The Spanish week starts on lunes, and the days are written in lowercase. Martes and miércoles are easy to swap; remember that miércoles, the longest name, sits in the middle of the week.

questions.question: Conjugate querer (to want) for yo.
questions.explanation: Querer is an e → ie stem-changing verb, so the stressed e of the stem becomes ie: quiero. Quero is the most common beginner mistake.

questions.question: Complete with pedir (to order): Nosotros ___ paella.
questions.explanation: Pedir changes e → i in the stressed forms (pido, pides, pide, piden), but in nosotros the stress falls on the ending, so the stem stays ped-: pedimos. Pidimos applies the change where it does not belong.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly says "I like the books"?
questions.explanation: The books are the subject of gustar, so the verb is plural, gustan, and the article stays: me gustan los libros. Me gusta los libros forgets the agreement, and yo gusto makes the speaker the thing that pleases.

questions.question: How do you say "Ana likes to dance"?
questions.explanation: The person goes in the pronoun le, often clarified with a Ana, and an activity in the infinitive takes singular gusta: A Ana le gusta bailar. Ana gusta bailar uses gustar like the English "like", which reverses the meaning.

questions.question: These words are shown without accents. Which one needs a written accent?
questions.explanation: Arbol ends in l, so by the rules its stress would fall on the last syllable, but it is said ÁR-bol. A written accent marks that exception: árbol. The other three follow the rules, so they need no accent.

questions.question: Translate into Spanish: It is one o'clock.
questions.explanation: One o'clock is singular, es la una, because it refers to una hora. Every other hour is plural: son las dos, son las tres. Son la una is the usual slip.

questions.question: Put these times in order, from earliest to latest.
questions.explanation: Menos subtracts minutes from the next hour: las ocho menos diez is 7:50 and las nueve menos cuarto is 8:45. Y adds them: y cuarto is 8:15 and y media is 8:30.

questions.question: Select every sentence that uses estar correctly.
choices: El libro está en la mesa.
La fiesta está en mi casa.
questions.explanation: Feelings (estoy cansada) and the location of people and things (está en la mesa, estamos en Madrid) take estar. A profession takes ser (es profesora), the location of an event takes ser (la fiesta es en mi casa), and the time takes ser (son las tres).

questions.question: Complete with jugar (to play): Mis hermanos ___ al fútbol los sábados.
questions.explanation: Jugar is the one u → ue stem-changer, and mis hermanos needs the ellos form: juegan. The -an ending is right because jugar is an -ar verb. Jugan forgets the stem change.
